analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas leasing and drilling.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2005 with four cosponsors, the bill never received a committee markup or floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the law that bans oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and required the Interior Department to hold lease sales in the refuge's coastal plain within about two years. It also would have pre-declared drilling 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose, limited the environmental review required before the first sale, and sent appeals straight to a single federal court with short deadlines. Half the revenue would go to Alaska, and a capped fund would aid affected local communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to lease and drill in a currently closed part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, with a mandated first sale of at least 200,000 acres of the most promising tracts [S2][S3]. Alaska would receive 50 percent of leasing and royalty revenue [S3], the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation would receive land conveyances [S2][S3], and affected Alaska communities would get impact aid from a fund capped at $15 million [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and Alaska Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Department to establish a competitive oil and gas leasing program in the ANWR coastal plain, repealing the statutory ban on production there [S2][S3].
Requires a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months of enactment and a second by September 2010 [S3].
Requires leases to carry at least a 12.5% royalty and a 2,000-acre cap on the surface footprint of development, with seasonal drilling limits to protect calving caribou and other wildlife [S3].

Sends 50% of bonus, rental, and royalty revenue to the State of Alaska and creates a Coastal Plain Local Government Impact Aid Assistance Fund, capped at $15 million, for affected communities including Kaktovik and the North Slope Borough [S3].
Requires lessees to negotiate project labor agreements for construction and production work, a provision benefiting organized labor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the loss of protection for the coastal plain of a national wildlife refuge, along with the environmental risks of industrial development there. The bill would declare drilling 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose by statute, count a 1987 environmental statement as satisfying the National Environmental Policy Act for pre-lease steps, forbid study of a no-leasing alternative, allow only a 20-day public comment window, and route legal challenges to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals under a presumption that the agency's analysis is correct [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the Arctic refuge itself

drawbacks.text: The bill would legislatively declare the leasing program 'compatible' with the refuge's established purposes and state that no further findings are required, removing the normal legal check that protects refuges from incompatible uses [S2][S3].

It would sharply narrow environmental review: the Secretary would not be required to identify or analyze non-leasing alternatives, public comments would be limited to 20 days on a single preferred action, and the agency's environmental analysis would be presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence in the D.C. Circuit within 90 days [S3].
Special protected 'Special Areas' would be capped at 45,000 acres of the coastal plain, and the Secretary could not close any coastal plain land to leasing except under the Act's own terms [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that drilling would industrialize a pristine part of the Arctic refuge, and that the bill's 'no significant adverse effect' standard, however strict on paper, would be enforced by an agency whose work the same bill shields from ordinary judicial review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real protections on paper — a surface footprint cap, seasonal drilling limits, reclamation liability, and revenue sharing with Alaska and local communities — but it built those protections into a framework that also repealed the production ban, pre-empted compatibility findings, truncated environmental review, and narrowed the courts' ability to second-guess the agency. For anyone who values the Arctic refuge's wilderness and wildlife, the central trade was permanent industrial access to the coastal plain in exchange for mitigation rules and local aid; the design tilted heavily toward making the leasing program hard to stop or slow once started.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in October 2005, and it never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Lisa Murkowski introduced the bill on October 19, 2005, on behalf of herself, Sens. Stevens, Akaka, and Inouye [S1][S3][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill sat in committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

The bill would have repealed the ANWR production ban in section 1003 of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act and mandated lease sales, with 50% of revenue to Alaska and a $15 million impact aid fund [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic refuge's coastal plain stayed legally closed to drilling, since the bill died before the production ban could be repealed. Oil companies gained nothing from this bill; anyone who wanted the refuge protected was better off because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Arctic refuge and its defenders

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the ANWR coastal plain to oil and gas leasing.

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Sens. Daniel Akaka and Daniel Inouye
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill two Democratic sponsors alongside two Republicans.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; chaired by Jeff Bingaman (D-NM)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or any action; it remained in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four original cosponsors split evenly between two Republicans and two Democrats, but no votes were ever taken, so the broader partisan divide never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would give the industry access to lease and drill in a national wildlife refuge that federal law currently bars from production, with a mandated first sale of the most promising tracts and streamlined environmental review. Its gains come from opening protected public land, a cost borne by the public.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation, Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill directs land conveyances to these corporations and requires local consultation, subsistence protections, and Native hiring efforts. The local impact aid fund would help small Arctic communities absorb development effects.
Alaska would receive 50% of leasing and royalty revenue, and a capped $15 million fund would aid Kaktovik, the North Slope Borough, and other affected communities.
Leases would have to require negotiation of project labor agreements for construction, maintenance, and production work, a win for organized labor.
